articles.title: Fiber optic cables reveal ‘icequakes’ in endangered glaciers
articles.content:
One of the hottest, most fascinating new fields in science doesn’t sound particularly exciting: distributed acoustic sensing, aka DAS. It involves using fiber optic cables to spy on the environment, and is proving to be enormously powerful. By analyzing the way that vibrations scatter light through the wires, scientists can detect volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, and even footsteps above. Last year, researchers laid a cable on the seafloor near a Greenland glacier, providing unprecedented insight into how the ice is rapidly deteriorating.



Now a team working in the mountains of Switzerland has used DAS to expose another troubling trend in ice, known as hydrofracturing, in which meltwater seeps deep down and creates pressure. By studying the phenomenon, scientists can get a better idea of how ice the world over will decline, and therefore better predict consequent problems like sea level rise.



“It’s hypothesized to be a mechanism that can cause mass disintegration of ice shelves and ice sheets in the Antarctic, Greenland, et cetera,” said Thomas Hudson, a seismologist at ETH­ Zurich in Switzerland and lead author of a recent paper describing the work. “But no one’s really observed the mechanism in any detail.”



For all its simplicity, DAS provides incredible amounts of data. On a Swiss alpine glacier, Hudson and his colleagues laid out fiber optic cables in a grid pattern. Then, using a device called an interrogator, they fired laser pulses through the cable. Even the tiniest of disturbances along the cable sent the tiniest bits of light back to the device, where they were logged.



A zoomed-in view of the grid of fiber optic cables (right) and its positioning on the glacier. Courtesy of Thomas Hudson

Using calculations based on the speed of light, the researchers could pinpoint an “icequake” — a fracture that generates seismic activity, similar to an earthquake — at different distances along the cable, since farther ones take ever so slightly longer to travel back. With an extensive grid pattern of cable, they detected vibrations in extreme detail. Compare this to a traditional seismometer, which detects shaking at a single point. “We can break that fiber optic cable into thousands of strain sensors,” Hudson said. “So, effectively equivalent to thousands of seismometers.”



In addition, fiber optic cables are relatively cheap, so if something catastrophic happened to the glacier, the researchers wouldn’t take as big of a financial hit. With all these crevasses around, glaciers can be extremely dangerous places for scientists to work. With DAS, though, they can lay the cable, leave the site, and get a constant stream of real-time data beamed from the interrogator.



“Whereas streaming data back from seismometers is not trivial, and then you have to process all the data back in your lab,” Hudson said. “DAS is actually more promising as a monitoring method, just purely from a data logistics point of view.”



Indeed, using DAS, the team found that this alpine glacier isn’t just threatened with melting from rising air temperatures. Because liquid water is denser than solid water, it flows deep down into cracks and forces the ice apart, creating crevasses that compromise the overall structural integrity. “How deep these cracks go, and how many cracks there are, really matter for the stability of the glacier,” Hudson said. “These glaciers overhang critical infrastructure like train lines or villages, and so it’s really important in the future to potentially apply this technology.”



Theoretically, a long-term DAS deployment could provide early warning of changes in stability. In just a week of this fieldwork, Hudson and his team detected more than a thousand icequakes. Furthermore, the resulting fractures allow meltwater to get deep into the glacier, which likely holds true for others beyond Switzerland.

One goal would be to develop DAS into an early-warning system for the kinds of catastrophic glacial collapses like what recently happened in Nepal. “I would be 99.999 percent certain that there were signals that you could pick up,” Hudson said of the disaster, though there would still be several steps to getting that information out in a way that would help protect people. “It’s still challenging, right? Our research still doesn’t address the question of how you turn the signals into an accurate early-warning system.”



DAS could also help monitor the ice in Greenland and Antarctica that is already collapsing into the world’s oceans. The issue isn’t so simple as the sun beating down on these ice sheets. In Antarctica especially, warming waters are eating at the undersides of ice shelves (the bits that float on the ocean), as underwater “storms” add more destructive turbulence. That other recent DAS study in Greenland found another dynamic: As ice violently calves, it stirs the water and breaks up an insulating layer of cold water resting against the ice, leading to still more melting — a sort of self-perpetuating cycle.



With DAS, scientists get an unprecedented look inside the ice, as seismic waves propagate and betray the destabilizing cracks. “If we can use this technology to understand how deep those cracks go,” Hudson said, “and how many cracks there are in the subsurface, then we will get a better idea of how stable those bigger glaciers are. And obviously that has implications for how fast these glaciers might break up and cause sea level rise.”
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant scientific advancement using fiber optic cables (DAS) to monitor glacier icequakes and hydrofracturing, providing critical insights into glacier stability and potential sea level rise. This technology offers a scalable, cost-effective way to monitor glaciers worldwide, with broad implications for climate change understanding and disaster preparedness, thus having a meaningful positive impact on society and the environment.
articles.personality_title: Fiber optic cables reveal hidden icequakes in glaciers
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists want to understand how glaciers are breaking apart because this affects sea levels and nearby communities. Traditional methods to study glaciers only give limited information from one spot.

**What happened** – Researchers in Switzerland used a technology called distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) with fiber optic cables laid in a grid on an alpine glacier. These cables detect tiny vibrations, called icequakes, caused by cracks forming in the ice. The cables send laser pulses and measure the light that bounces back to locate where the ice is cracking.

**Impact** – This method acts like thousands of sensors along the glacier, giving detailed and real-time data about ice fractures. It helps scientists better understand how meltwater forces cracks deep into the glacier, weakening it. This insight is important because glaciers can threaten infrastructure like train lines and villages. DAS is also cheaper and safer than traditional tools, allowing continuous monitoring without needing scientists to stay on dangerous glaciers.

**What's next step** – The researchers hope to use DAS to create early warning systems for glacier collapses that can endanger people and property. They also plan to study glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica to better predict sea level rise caused by melting ice. The technology could help track how cracks grow and how glaciers become unstable over time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using fiber optic cables to detect icequakes gives scientists a powerful new way to watch glaciers break apart, improving safety and climate predictions.

articles.title: The legendary snow leopard comes up against harsh realities in remarkable book
articles.summary: In Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi's The Ghost of the Mountains, the near-spiritual myth of the elusive snow leopard becomes a way of understanding all that we stand to lose from the forces of climate change
articles.content:
In Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi's The Ghost of the Mountains, the near-spiritual myth of the elusive snow leopard becomes a way of understanding all that we stand to lose from the forces of climate change

Snow leopards’ coats help them vanish against boulders and scree Francois Savigny/naturepl.com

The Ghost of the Mountains

Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi

Granta Books (UK); Riverhead Books (US)

Like many large carnivores, the snow leopard is eclipsed by an outsize reputation, which makes it almost impossible to separate the animal from the story. The solitary, largely silent cat is often spoken of as being not there – a shadow, a ghost – with its ethereal presence, in the Buddhist heartlands of the Himalaya, bordering on the spiritual.

When Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi first proposed studying the cat, his professor dismissed the idea, because, he said, his student would never see one. Yet two decades on (and a handful of sightings later), Suryawanshi has produced a wonderful book, The Ghost of the Mountains, about this most unknowable of animals.

Advertisement

During the Pleistocene ice age, the snow leopard’s distribution probably stretched from Portugal to Siberia. But their range contracted with the ice, and they are now confined to 12 countries in Central Asia and the Himalaya, across some of the world’s highest mountain ranges. Unlike wolves, say, or lynxes, they are the only large carnivores to be exclusively adapted to mountains. Their dusky coats, spotted with dark rosettes, vanish against boulders and scree. Relative to their body size, their tails are longer than that of any other cat, helping them balance, while wide nostrils warm the air they breathe. Genetic adaptations let them cope with the thin air.

The leopard becomes his way of penetrating the complexity and fragility of all we stand to lose

Suryawanshi is equally well equipped to study them, combining profound patience, a lifetime of mountaineering and a deep passion for this enigmatic animal. This is just as well: it is hard to imagine a more punishing environment for fieldwork. The snow leopard inhabits 3 million square kilometres of mountains. The peaks soar to over 8000 metres and the weather can turn on a dime. His teams must deal with hypothermia, blizzards, bears and rivers in spate. One friend dies of a heart attack, a complication of altitude sickness. Another, who worked to protect the mountains from mining, is found dead, his death unexplained.

Until Suryawanshi began his work, less than 1 per cent of the snow leopard’s habitat had been properly surveyed. Yet it is impossible to conserve something if you cannot show that it is there.

As far as we know, a snow leopard has never harmed a human, the only big cat to hold this “noble record”. Yet this still hasn’t endeared the cats to the herders that share their hills. As I wrote in my own work on wolves in Europe, conservation achieves little without a meaningful, concurrent approach to coexistence. Killing snow leopards is illegal, but that doesn’t stop poaching.

Yet predators aren’t the only threat to these livelihoods. When mining companies prospect for mineral deposits in the Gobi desert, Suryawanshi’s team discovers that under Mongolian law, holders of traditional land rights can form nature reserves by demonstrating the biodiversity of the land. Working with herders, procuring funds for them to build corrals to keep their goats safe, the team sets about changing the narrative of the snow leopard, and ultimately enables the formation of the Tost-Tosonbumba Nature Reserve. It is those who live there, Suryawanshi understands, who are the land’s most vital custodians.

Writing about the snow leopard inevitably means writing about naturalist and writer Peter Matthiessen. In 1973, he was invited by the naturalist George Schaller to accompany him to the Inner Dolpa on the Tibetan plateau of Nepal, on a search for the snow leopard. Matthiessen never sees one, but his book about the journey did much to cement the animal’s mythology as both remarkable carnivore and potent symbol of the untamed and the ineffable.

For Suryawanshi, too, the snow leopard is his way into these places. But if for Matthiessen the elusive animal becomes a cipher for the mystery at the heart of oneself, for Suryawanshi, the quest is far more tangible. The snow leopard becomes his way of penetrating the complexity and fragility of ecosystems and human cultures, and all we stand to lose.

One of the great merits of the book is its story of conservation from a non-Western perspective. Two decades ago, when Suryawanshi began his work, the snow leopard was little studied and the majority of researchers were Westerners. In one illuminating chapter, he explores the downlisting of the snow leopard from “endangered” to “vulnerable” in 2017 by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. Whether such a downlisting is merited depends on estimating the population, a Herculean task, and so decisions become politicised. While Western scientists broadly support the downlisting, claiming a conservation success, local scientists fear it will embolden those who want to develop the mountains. Suryawanshi brings a rare, much needed reminder that “political and racial bias” remains in how the wider academic community sees local researchers.

“If there is still a mystery left in the Himalaya,” says one mountain ranger, early in the book, “then it is the snow leopard.” Something similar could have been claimed for Everest, but the mountain is now “for tourists”, says one mountaineering instructor. A boom in wildlife tourism risks similar commodification of snow leopards. With dedicated guides and telemetric equipment, they are now easier to find and Suryawanshi has a certain disdain for photographers lined up to grab a photo of the ghost. Yet tourists bring money to communities and add weight to the idea that these animals and their habitats carry intrinsic value worth protecting.

In the end, Suryawanshi writes, “whether local livestock herders chose to live with snow leopards would depend on their own stories”. Towards the end of the book, an ancient male snow leopard lies down outside a mountain village. Decades earlier, a herder would have killed him on the spot. But now the villagers see him differently. They leave out meat, and when he dies, they bring him into the village and give him a funeral. People can change, if their concerns are understood. It is a remarkable moment in a remarkable book about this most inscrutable of animals.

Adam Weymouth is a writer based in Kent, UK

articles.title: Designer floating homes may be the future as sea levels rise
articles.summary: Are these floating houses in Amsterdam’s IJburg district the shape of things to come? Check out Floating Futures, a new series by photojournalist Alessandro Gandolfi
articles.content:
Are these floating houses in Amsterdam’s IJburg district the shape of things to come? Check out Floating Futures, a new series by photojournalist Alessandro Gandolfi

Floating houses at the edge of Amsterdam, shot by Alessandro Gandolfi for his photo essay Floating Futures Alessandro Gandolfi/Panos Pictures

Floating Futures

Alessandro Gandolfi

Imagine a city where suburbs float on water. Floating homes already exist in coastal communities in places like the Philippines and Vietnam. Now, high-income nations facing dangerous sea-level rise are looking to those examples.

Among them is the Netherlands, where over a quarter of the land is below sea level and around two-thirds of it is at risk of flooding.

Advertisement

This photograph shows floating houses in the IJburg district at the edge of Amsterdam, the largest Dutch city. The image comes from Floating Futures, a new series by photojournalist Alessandro Gandolfi.

The affluent, relatively high-density IJburg community comprises 158 waterside homes, 55 of which are floating. Residents are connected by bridges and roads, and most houses have a boat outside instead of a car.

Simply raising the dykes is no longer enough against the rising waters, Gandolfi writes in his photo essay. “Experts warn that mastering water’s whims is an illusion. The answer, they say, lies in a shift of mindset – the philosophy of meebewegen: not fighting against water, but learning to live with it.”

The homes at IJburg aren’t houseboats or retrofitted vessels like the ones lining Amsterdam’s canals, but architect-designed homes intended to encourage community living. They are built to be sustainable, with rooftop solar panels and careful management of sewage and other waste.

But their biggest difference from other houses will always lie below, in their watery foundations.

This shows a new way to adapt to climate change by living with water instead of trying to fight it.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Floating homes in Amsterdam offer a smart, sustainable way to live safely as sea levels rise.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les maisons flottantes d’Amsterdam, une nouvelle façon de vivre avec la montée des eaux
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreuses villes côtières sont menacées par la montée du niveau de la mer, qui met en danger les habitations et les communautés. Les Pays-Bas sont particulièrement exposés car une grande partie du territoire est sous le niveau de la mer et sujette aux inondations.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Dans le quartier IJburg d’Amsterdam, 55 maisons flottantes font partie des 158 maisons au bord de l’eau. Ces maisons sont conçues pour flotter sur l’eau, reliées par des ponts et des routes, et les habitants utilisent souvent des bateaux au lieu de voitures. Le photographe Alessandro Gandolfi a pris des photos de ces maisons dans une nouvelle série appelée Floating Futures.

**Impact** – Ces maisons flottantes ne sont pas de simples péniches. Elles sont conçues par des architectes pour favoriser la vie en communauté et incluent des panneaux solaires sur le toit ainsi qu’une gestion intelligente des déchets. Cela montre une nouvelle façon de s’adapter au changement climatique en vivant avec l’eau plutôt qu’en la combattant.

**Prochaine étape** – Avec la montée continue des eaux, d’autres régions pourraient construire des maisons flottantes comme celles d’IJburg. Cela pourrait changer la façon dont les villes se préparent à l’avenir et protègent leurs habitants des inondations.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les maisons flottantes d’Amsterdam offrent une solution intelligente et durable pour vivre en sécurité face à la montée des eaux.

Esto muestra una nueva forma de adaptarse al cambio climático viviendo con el agua en lugar de luchar contra ella.

**Próximo paso** – A medida que sube el nivel del mar, más lugares podrían construir casas flotantes como las de IJburg. Esto podría cambiar la forma en que las ciudades planean su futuro y protegen a sus habitantes de las inundaciones.

articles.title: Climate attribution science just changed the rules for fossil fuel lawsuits

The post Climate attribution science just changed the rules for fossil fuel lawsuits first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Scientists can now draw a straight line from a single oil company’s emissions to a specific disaster. Not a rough estimate of the industry’s overall contribution, but a specific company, a specific event, a specific percentage.

That’s what a new peer-reviewed study published in Earth’s Future has done, and the fossil fuel industry is paying attention, because their defense in climate lawsuits has always been that causation is impossible to prove. Christopher Callahan’s work punches a hole in that argument.

Callahan, an Earth systems scientist and assistant professor at Indiana University’s O’Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs, ran more than 150 simulations across eight different climate models, building a statistical map of the relationship between atmospheric carbon dioxide and the odds of extreme heat and rainfall. He then plugged in historical emissions data from individual companies and countries.

The numbers he got are not minor. Fossil fuel firms increased the likelihood of the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat wave by 31 percent. They raised the probability of Pakistan’s catastrophic 2022 extreme rainfall by seven percent. “There is no level of emissions that does not contribute to changing climate impacts,” Callahan said. “Every ton matters.”

Why source attribution is different

Climate attribution science has been around for over two decades. Its core question: how much did human-caused warming increase the odds of a given event? Source attribution goes narrower and asks which specific actors caused which specific effects.

Answering that used to mean linking multiple climate models together in processes that could take months and required significant computing resources. Callahan’s approach bypasses that. Because the relationship between cumulative emissions and warming follows predictable proportions, he can calculate each emitter’s contribution to a specific event using historical data alone.

“What this science tells us,” Callahan explained, “is that there is a direct relationship between how much an entity emits and the extreme events that alter people’s lives.”

Kim Cobb, an observational climate expert at Brown University, called it “extremely valuable” and noted it “would have been a pipe dream 10 years ago; it simply wouldn’t be possible.” Jim Hurrell, a professor of atmospheric science at Colorado State University and chair of the National Academies’ recent extreme weather report, is less focused on the courts than on what comes after. “This science could be really useful to help communities plan for the future,” he said.

A missing piece for climate lawsuits

More than 40 climate lawsuits have been filed against major oil companies in the US since 2017, brought by states, municipalities, and tribal governments. At least five have entered the discovery phase, where executives could be forced to hand over internal documents and testify under oath about what the companies knew and when.

The sticking point in most of these cases has been causation. At a 2025 Federalist Society panel on climate litigation, Michael Buschbacher, a partner at Boyden Gray PLLC who has backed industry opposition to climate liability laws, put the challenge plainly: “How do you show that emissions from company X cause injury Y from a hurricane or whatever?”

Callahan’s study is a direct response to that. Even Kyle Kohli, writing in Energy In Depth, a publication of the Independent Petroleum Association of America, acknowledged what this science represents for plaintiffs: “Climate attribution research seeks to connect greenhouse-gas emissions to specific climate impacts, and increasingly, to particular industries or companies. That makes it especially valuable to climate plaintiffs attempting to overcome one of their biggest legal obstacles: proving causation.”

The American Petroleum Institute listed stopping “extreme climate liability policy” as one of its top 2026 priorities. It is a harder problem to solve than it used to be.

The campaign against the research

The fossil fuel industry has known about its role in warming the planet for more than 50 years. Its long-running response has been to fund doubt wherever the science gained traction. A June investigation by Politico found a secret campaign by oil industry allies to discredit a National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report on extreme weather attribution, coming just months after Republican attorneys general successfully forced the removal of a NAS climate sciences chapter from a reference manual for federal judges.

A NASA scientist who asked not to be named called the decision to pull the chapter “pathetic. If they cannot stand up for science, then who is going to?”

Researchers themselves are not divided on the findings. Michael Mann, a climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, called the NAS report “great” and said it “didn’t pull any punches.” Kristina Dahl, a climate scientist and vice president for science at Climate Central, described it as “a really excellent roundup of the state of the science.”

Callahan is clear-eyed about where his research sits politically. “Our responsibility as scientists is not to never do science that is relevant to the political conversation,” he said. “We should follow the results of our questions wherever they lead and report them regardless of what they are.”

Climate scientist Yann Quilcaille of ETH Zürich put it plainly: “We need to act quickly, and we have the solutions.”

articles.personality_title: New science links oil companies to specific climate disasters
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long studied how human activities cause climate change and make extreme weather more likely. But it was hard to prove that one company’s pollution caused a specific disaster.

**What happened** – A new study by Christopher Callahan, published in the journal Earth’s Future, has found a way to connect emissions from individual fossil fuel companies to particular extreme weather events. Using many computer simulations and data from past emissions, Callahan showed, for example, that fossil fuel companies made the 2021 heat wave in the Pacific Northwest 31% more likely and increased the chance of Pakistan’s 2022 heavy rains by 7%.

**Impact** – This method is important because it can show exactly how much a single company’s pollution contributes to a specific disaster. This is different from older studies that only estimated the total effect of all humans. Now, courts can use this science to hold companies responsible for the harm their emissions cause. It also helps communities understand risks and plan for the future.

**What's next step** – More climate lawsuits against oil companies may use this new science to prove cause and effect. This could change legal battles and push companies to reduce pollution faster. Scientists will continue refining these methods, and communities might use the findings to prepare better for extreme weather.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New research can now link a single fossil fuel company’s emissions directly to specific extreme weather events, helping hold polluters accountable and improve climate planning.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle science relie les compagnies pétrolières à des catastrophes climatiques précises
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient depuis longtemps comment les activités humaines causent le changement climatique et rendent les phénomènes météorologiques extrêmes plus fréquents. Mais il était difficile de prouver que la pollution d’une seule entreprise provoquait une catastrophe précise.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une nouvelle étude de Christopher Callahan, publiée dans la revue Earth’s Future, a trouvé un moyen de relier les émissions des compagnies fossiles individuelles à des événements climatiques extrêmes spécifiques. Grâce à de nombreuses simulations informatiques et aux données historiques, Callahan a montré, par exemple, que les compagnies fossiles ont augmenté de 31 % la probabilité de la vague de chaleur de 2021 dans le Nord-Ouest du Pacifique et de 7 % celle des fortes pluies au Pakistan en 2022.

**Impact** – Cette méthode est importante car elle peut montrer exactement combien la pollution d’une seule entreprise contribue à une catastrophe précise. C’est différent des études plus anciennes qui estimaient seulement l’effet total de tous les humains. Désormais, les tribunaux peuvent utiliser cette science pour tenir les entreprises responsables des dégâts causés. Cela aide aussi les communautés à mieux comprendre les risques et à se préparer.

**Prochaine étape** – Plus de procès climatiques contre les compagnies pétrolières pourraient utiliser cette nouvelle science pour prouver la cause et l’effet. Cela pourrait changer les batailles juridiques et pousser les entreprises à réduire plus vite leur pollution. Les scientifiques continueront à améliorer ces méthodes, et les communautés pourront mieux se préparer aux événements extrêmes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une nouvelle recherche permet désormais de relier directement les émissions d’une seule compagnie fossile à des événements climatiques extrêmes précis, aidant à responsabiliser les pollueurs et à mieux planifier le climat.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva ciencia vincula a compañías petroleras con desastres climáticos específicos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han estudiado durante mucho tiempo cómo las actividades humanas causan el cambio climático y hacen que los eventos climáticos extremos sean más probables. Pero era difícil probar que la contaminación de una sola empresa causara un desastre específico.

**Qué pasó** – Un nuevo estudio de Christopher Callahan, publicado en la revista Earth’s Future, encontró una manera de conectar las emisiones de compañías de combustibles fósiles individuales con eventos climáticos extremos específicos. Usando muchas simulaciones por computadora y datos históricos, Callahan mostró, por ejemplo, que las compañías fósiles aumentaron en un 31 % la probabilidad de la ola de calor de 2021 en el noroeste del Pacífico y en un 7 % la posibilidad de las fuertes lluvias en Pakistán en 2022.

**Impacto** – Este método es importante porque puede mostrar exactamente cuánto contribuye la contaminación de una sola empresa a un desastre específico. Esto es diferente de estudios anteriores que solo estimaban el efecto total de todos los humanos. Ahora, los tribunales pueden usar esta ciencia para responsabilizar a las empresas por los daños causados. También ayuda a las comunidades a entender mejor los riesgos y a prepararse.

**Próximo paso** – Más demandas climáticas contra compañías petroleras podrían usar esta nueva ciencia para probar causa y efecto. Esto podría cambiar las batallas legales y presionar a las empresas para que reduzcan la contaminación más rápido. Los científicos seguirán mejorando estos métodos y las comunidades podrán prepararse mejor para eventos climáticos extremos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Una nueva investigación ahora puede vincular directamente las emisiones de una sola compañía de combustibles fósiles con eventos climáticos extremos específicos, ayudando a responsabilizar a los contaminadores y a mejorar la planificación climática.
